say.text: Day 1 after total thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma. She is comfortable, her voice is normal and her neck is quiet.
Across patients after total thyroidectomy, which complication is the most common?

choices.label: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, causing hoarseness
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Separate the complication that frightens the team from the one that happens most often. Count patients, not fear.
That choice is not right. Nerve injury is the complication surgeons fear most, so it feels like the everyday one.
Feared is not the same as frequent. Hoarseness from a palsy is a real risk, but it is not the complication most patients get.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Dramatic complications feel common. Check frequency separately from how frightening a complication is.

say.text: That choice is not right. A neck haematoma is dangerous and urgent, so it feels like the complication you meet most.
A haematoma that compresses the airway is an emergency. Emergency and frequency are separate questions.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Urgent and common are different questions; keep them apart.

say.text: Frequency and danger are different questions. Transient hypocalcaemia is the most common complication.
It usually shows in the first 24–72 hours as perioral tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and tetany.
Yes. Transient hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism is the most common complication after total thyroidectomy.
Watch for perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign, usually in the first 24–72 hours.
Two days after total thyroidectomy, a singer says her voice tires quickly and she can no longer reach her high notes.
She has no hoarseness and no noisy breathing. Which nerve injury is most likely?

choices.label: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve on one side
Both recurrent laryngeal nerves, on each side
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pitch depends on tension in the cords, not on how they move. Which nerve supplies the muscle that tenses them?
That choice is not right. Recurrent nerve palsy is the best-known voice injury, so any voice change feels like it.
Hoarseness is the recurrent nerve sign. This singer has no hoarseness, so the pattern points elsewhere.

sure_note.text: You were sure. One nerve for every voice change is the model to drop. Test each symptom against its own nerve.

say.text: That choice is not right. Both nerves lie in the same field, so a two-sided injury sounds like a bigger version of the same problem.
Bilateral palsy is the airway problem, with stridor. This singer breathes normally, so that pattern does not fit.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Match the nerve to the symptom it produces, not to how serious the surgery looked.

say.text: Loss of high pitch and voice fatigue come from paralysis of the cricothyroid, which the external branch supplies.
Hoarseness points to the recurrent nerve, and stridor to bilateral palsy. Each sign has its own nerve.
Yes. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid, the muscle that tenses the cords for pitch.
Loss of high pitch and voice fatigue point to it. Hoarseness is the recurrent nerve sign, a different pattern.
Six hours after thyroidectomy, your patient has a tense, swollen neck and noisy breathing with each breath.
What is your first action?

choices.label: Intubate the patient on the ward before any other step
Transfer to the operating theatre before any other step
Open the wound at the bedside to evacuate the clot
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what is pressing on the airway from outside, and what would take that pressure off.
That choice is not right. Protecting the airway is the first reflex, so a tube feels like the safe default.
Here the swelling compresses the airway from outside, so the cause must be relieved first.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Airway first is a good rule, but check what is blocking the airway before you choose the device.

say.text: That choice is not right. The theatre has the best equipment, so moving first feels like the responsible step.
A tense swelling can close the airway while the patient is moved, and the move takes time the airway may not have.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Ask what threatens the airway now, not where the best setting is.

say.text: A haematoma compressing the airway is released first: open the wound at the bedside and evacuate the clot.
After that, secure the airway as needed. Bilateral recurrent nerve palsy also causes stridor and may need reintubation or tracheostomy.
Yes. A tense haematoma compresses the airway from outside, so the wound is opened at the bedside and the clot evacuated.
Stridor can also come from bilateral recurrent nerve palsy, which needs a different first step.
A patient has two voice complaints after thyroidectomy: she is hoarse, and she has lost her high notes.
Which pairing of nerve and symptom is right?

choices.label: Hoarseness with the recurrent nerve; pitch loss with the external branch
Hoarseness with the external branch; pitch loss with the recurrent nerve
Both complaints come from the unilateral recurrent nerve alone
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Each symptom has its own nerve. Ask which movement each nerve controls: moving the cords, or tensing them.
That choice is not right. Both complaints are voice changes, so the two nerves are easy to swap in memory.
Recheck which muscle each nerve works through before you pair the signs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the nerve-to-muscle link before you attach a symptom to a nerve.

say.text: That choice is not right. Recurrent nerve palsy is the best-known voice injury, so it feels like the cause of every voice change.
Not every voice change comes from that nerve. Loss of pitch has its own nerve, the external branch.

sure_note.text: You were sure. One nerve for every voice change is the model to drop; test each sign on its own.

say.text: Hoarseness points to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Loss of high pitch and voice fatigue point to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, from paralysis of the cricothyroid.
Yes. Hoarseness is the recurrent laryngeal nerve sign. Loss of high pitch comes from the external branch.
The external branch injury paralyses the cricothyroid muscle, and that is what drops the pitch.
Day 1 after thyroidectomy, your patient has noisy breathing. Her neck is soft and flat, with no swelling under the wound.
Which first step fits her?

choices.label: Open the wound at the bedside to evacuate a clot
Secure the airway now, then look for the cause
Transfer to the theatre to explore the neck first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask first what is blocking the airway. Then ask whether that cause sits in the neck you can see.
That choice is not right. Opening the neck fixed the earlier patient, so it feels like the default for any noisy breathing.
Opening the wound helps when a clot is the cause. Check what is actually narrowing this airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check that the cause is in the neck before you cut into it.

say.text: That choice is not right. A theatre gives the best control, so moving first feels like the careful choice.
The airway is the immediate threat, and a move takes time it may not have.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Ask what threatens the airway now, not where the best setting is.

say.text: With a flat neck there is no tense clot to release. Secure the airway by reintubation or tracheostomy.
Opening the wound is for a tense haematoma compressing the airway. Bilateral palsy is the other cause of stridor.
Yes. Bilateral recurrent nerve palsy can cause stridor and airway obstruction, and needs reintubation or tracheostomy.
A flat neck has no clot to release, so the airway is the problem to fix now. Then look for the cause.
A junior tells you the commonest complication after thyroidectomy is bleeding, because bleeding is the one that frightens everyone.
Which pairing do you tell the junior is right?

choices.label: Haematoma is the commonest; hypocalcaemia is the feared one
Nerve palsy is the commonest; haematoma is the feared one
Hypocalcaemia is the commonest; haematoma is the feared one
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Keep two questions apart: which complication happens most often, and which one is most dangerous.
That choice is not right. Bleeding can threaten the airway quickly, so it feels like the one that happens most.
Danger and frequency are separate questions. A haematoma that compresses the airway is an emergency, but it is not the most frequent.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Keep 'most common' for frequency and 'most feared' for risk.

say.text: That choice is not right. Nerve injury is the complication surgeons fear most, so it feels like the everyday one.
Nerve palsy is a real complication, with hoarseness or airway risk. It is not the commonest one.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The nerve is the feared structure, not the frequent one.

say.text: The commonest complication is transient hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism, usually within 24–72 hours.
Haematoma and nerve palsy are feared because they threaten the airway or voice, not because they are most frequent.
Yes. Transient hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism is the most common complication after total thyroidectomy.
Haematoma is the one to act on fast, because it compresses the airway and needs the wound opened.
Six months after total thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma, the lab sends two results back.
Calcitonin is normal. Serum thyroglobulin has risen since the last review. Which result should prompt a recurrence work-up?

choices.label: The normal calcitonin, since it rules out a cancer
Both results equally, since both are tumour markers
A rising thyroglobulin level, which suggests recurrence
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which cancer each marker tracks, and whether a normal result of the other marker can answer the question here.
That choice is not right. A normal tumour marker feels reassuring, and calcitonin is the thyroid marker most people remember.
Calcitonin marks medullary carcinoma from the parafollicular cell, so a normal value says little about papillary cancer.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check which cancer a marker tracks before a normal result reassures you.

say.text: That choice is not right. Both are tumour markers, so reading them as one test feels efficient.
Each marker tracks its own cancer, so the two results do not carry the same meaning.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read each marker against its own cancer before you combine them.

say.text: Thyroglobulin is the follow-up marker for papillary and follicular cancer. A rising or detectable level suggests recurrence.
Calcitonin belongs to medullary carcinoma, and CEA is listed with it, not with differentiated cancer.
Yes. Serum thyroglobulin is the tumour marker for recurrence after total thyroidectomy, and a rising level suggests it.
Calcitonin is a different marker, for medullary carcinoma. Keep each marker with its own cancer.
